Is there no instance?

example (α : Type*) [Preorder α] :
    let := Preorder.topology α; OrderTopology α :=
    let := Preorder.topology α; ⟨rfl⟩
this would fire on every OrderTopology goal, right?

so it's a perf thing?
in that case, my question is: what's the canonical way to put the order topology on an ordered type?
within a proof, I mean - if it appears in the statement then we can just assume [TopologicalSpace X] [OrderTopology X] without losing generality

you can just

  let := Preorder.topology α
  have : OrderTopology α := ⟨rfl⟩

OK - this is what I have been doing but I thought that surely there's a better way
like we have algebraize for this issue with towers of extensions

and in general we have the instances apply automatically
maybe we should have a non-instance reducible def? Preorder.topology.orderTopology
wouldn't it still fire on every OrderTopology goal? I don't see how that helps

not an instance, just a theorem (I said reducible def my bad)

let := Preorder.topology α
have := Preorder.topology.orderTopology α

way better for discoverability
I thought I was doing something wrong because I went into the internals!

relatedly:

example {F : Type*} [GroupWithZero F] {x : F} (hx : x ≠ 0) :
  Invertible x := (Units.mk0 _ hx).invertible

is there a non-instance def for this? I couldn't find one
docs#invertibleOfNonzero

FWIW with the module topology (a canonical topology on a module over a topological ring) I have been doing exactly what you suggest above -- if I want one in a statement I do [TopologicalSpace M] [IsModuleTopology R M] and if I want one in a proof I do let : TopologicalSpace M := moduleTopology R M; have : IsModuleTopology R M := \<rfl\>. I agree that one could have a besopke tactic for these sorts of thing.
Not sure what the functionality of such a tactic would look like, but let's definitely add these theorems for discoverability, and document why they're not instances.

The rfl solution doesn't work when there are different topologies in the context, right?
Much like measure-theory theorems take in an arbitrary Measure instead of using the canonical ℙ, should we restate topology lemmas using IsOpen[Preorder.topology α] s instead of assuming OrderTopology?

Then it wouldn't apply to cases where the topology is gotten another way, for example the topology on Real is the order topology but it's defined as the metric topology, and then it's a theorem that they're the same.

I'm not sure what you mean @Snir Broshi. The application I had in mind is putting a topology on a type with no topology on it (eg because I have a purely algebraic statement about an ordered field but my proof uses the order topology on it).

Artie Khovanov said:

I'm not sure what you mean

For example, this is a very strange proof:

import Mathlib
open Topology
example : Preorder.topology ℕ ≤ lowerSet ℕ := by
  intro s hs
  let := lowerSet ℕ
  have hs' : IsLowerSet s := IsLowerSet.isOpen_iff_isLowerSet.mp hs
  let := Preorder.topology ℕ
  let : OrderTopology ℕ := ⟨rfl⟩
  exact hs'.isOpen

It should be just fun s hs ↦ IsLowerSet.isOpen_iff_isLowerSet.mp hs |>.isOpen but that doesn't work.

Aaron Liu said:

you can just

  let := Preorder.topology α
  have : OrderTopology α := ⟨rfl⟩

surely the principled way is by creating a type alias (for endowing a type with the order topology)?

In concrete applications, sure
But I mean this is for a generic lemma
How would I (easily) use a type alias to help prove "a polynomial over an ordered field tends to infinity at infinity"? Assuming the proof uses eg the continuity of polynomials wrt the order topology.

Yeah, the principled way if there's not a topology already on the object in the statement of the theorem and there are no other topologies you care about on the object in the proof, is just to put the topology you want on the object in the proof.

There are examples in the module topology API where one is trying to prove results of the form "if M and N have the module topology then the product topology on M x N considered as a module is the module topology" and here a type alias is useful, because M x N wants the product topology whereas you definitely need to talk about the object with the module topology. But for Artie's proof a type alias makes no sense.
Yes, the distinction is whether the topology appears in the statement

So does anyone have suggestions for my proof, or is it the best we can do? Juggling topologies like this seems wrong, and there are probably other theorems that have to have much more switcheroos.

btw docs#WithTopology is a generic type-alias, which saves creating your own in many cases

I mean, fundamentally sometimes a proof will use data not available in the statement. It happens that we write the definition of "tends to infinity" without using topology, but the most general proof technique is likely to be topological.
I don't see this as any different to classical or algebraize. The issue to me is the UX of constructing and using the topology.

IIUC we don't put the order topology on just any poset (even in a scope) because there are other natural topologies we might use. In that case, the definition of "tends to infinity" is no longer faithful to the topology (for instance, it's no longer the inverse of "tends to zero from the right"). So arguably the issue here is that we can even state "tends to infinity" without mentioning the order topology!

I think the answer here is just to use docs#WithTopology in the proof, along with, presumably, the identity order isomorphism between α and WithTopology α τ. This avoids defeq abuse and avoids let and have.
I really think this is the wrong design. That means transferring over an arbitrary amount of algebraic instances, rather than just constructing a single topological one.

Artie Khovanov said:

So arguably the issue here is that we can even state "tends to infinity" without mentioning the order topology!

That's not weird? For instance, it's absolutely essential that we can use the atTop filter on Finset ι without having a topology on ι (for use with docs#HasSum).

TBC I'm not advocating for changing the definition - my point is just that our definition of "tends to infinity" is implicitly aligned with the order topology.
And it would be a topology on Finset ι, not a topology on ι. Indeed we can (but shouldn't by default) put the order topology on Finset ι.

Artie Khovanov said:

my point is just that our definition of "tends to infinity" is implicitly aligned with the order topology

I don't know what you mean by this? Can you make it precise please?

We define docs#Filter.atTop by taking all the open +ve rays. In particular:

  • the inverse of atTop is 𝓝[>] 0 in the order topology.
  • Tendsto f l atTop is equivalent to Tendsto f l (𝓝 ⊤) if we pass to WithTop and use the order topology.
atTop is all the closed +ve rays
oh is it? well it's equivalent in an unbounded above order, right
it's equivalent in a NoMaxOrder
We have docs#Filter.atTop_eq_generate_Ici, and docs#Filter.atTop_basis_Ioi' that requires IsDirectedOrder in addition to NoMaxOrder

Artie Khovanov said:

We define docs#Filter.atTop by taking all the open +ve rays. In particular:

  • the inverse of atTop is 𝓝[>] 0 in the order topology.
  • Tendsto f l atTop is equivalent to Tendsto f l (𝓝 ⊤) if we pass to WithTop and use the order topology.

Thanks. The first one requires a lot of additional structure, so I don't take that as evidence, but the second makes sense. At the same time, it doesn't seem particularly useful for the kinds of things you're talking about since you are likely not passing to WithTop very often?

But let me return to docs#WithTopology. You claim:
Artie Khovanov said:

I really think this is the wrong design. That means transferring over an arbitrary amount of algebraic instances, rather than just constructing a single topological one.

While true, I suspect that in practice you won't need "an arbitrary amount", but "a handful of". Moreover, for type synonyms we generally transfer these instances over anyway. We haven't done this for algebraic structures for WithTopology yet because it is only a few months old, but I think it's totally reasonable to do so. Moreover, once we do, then the argument I described would be pretty much painless.

thanks for explaining

Do you know about all the docs#Equiv.field type instances we have? This is the way to transfer the algebraic instances over. It should only be a very small amount of work.

theorem Filter.tendsto_iff_tendsto_inv_inv {α β : Type*} [InvolutiveInv α]
    (f : α → β) (l : Filter α) (m : Filter β) :
    Tendsto f l m ↔ Tendsto (fun x ↦ f x⁻¹) l⁻¹ m := by
  simp_rw [tendsto_def, mem_inv]
  convert Iff.rfl
  ext
  simp

theorem Polynomial.tendsto_atTop_of_leadingCoeff_nonneg
    (hdeg : 0 < P.degree) (hlcf : 0 ≤ P.leadingCoeff) :
    Tendsto P.eval atTop atTop := by
  let := Preorder.topology F
  have := Preorder.topology.orderTopology F
  rw [tendsto_iff_tendsto_inv_inv, inv_atTop₀,
  tendsto_congr' (f₂ := (fun x ↦ P.reverse.eval x * x⁻¹ ^ P.natDegree))]
  ...
